common_name: Roy Hartley Begonia (Apricot Camellia-Flowered Tuberous Begonia)

planting.note: Start tubers indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, hollow-side up in moist peat or seed compost, then move to pots or beds after frost danger has passed, in bright, filtered shade.

directions: Grow in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil or container mix in bright shade to filtered morning sun, sheltered from wind. Roy Hartley is a classic upright exhibition tuberous begonia bred by the English firm Blackmore & Langdon, producing huge, fully double, camellia-form flowers in soft apricot-salmon shading to yellow at the base of the petals, held above sturdy, well-foliaged stems. As with other large-flowered tuberous types, it benefits from disbudding the two smaller female side buds beside each main male flower to channel energy into larger blooms, and from staking to support the heavy flower heads. Feed with a high-potash fertilizer through summer to sustain bloom size and color. Where winters are too cold to leave tubers in the ground, lift after foliage yellows in fall, cure, and store the dry tubers in a frost-free location for replanting the following spring.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants after all frost danger has passed in partial shade to morning sun, in moist, fertile, well-drained soil or potting mix; unlike most hybrid fuchsias, this triphylla-type selection tolerates considerably more heat and direct sun.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil or container mix in partial shade to morning sun. Gartenmeister Bonstedt, raised in Germany in the early twentieth century, bears velvety bronze-green foliage and long, narrow, tubular flowers in rich orange-red rather than the two-toned skirted bells of typical hybrid fuchsias, produced in clusters at the branch tips from summer into fall. Its triphylla parentage gives it markedly better heat and humidity tolerance than most fuchsia hybrids, making it one of the most reliable fuchsias for hot, muggy Gulf Coast summers, and its tubular blooms are a strong hummingbird draw. Pinch young plants to encourage a fuller, more floriferous habit, and feed regularly through the growing season. Treat as an annual or overwinter cuttings indoors in zones below 9-10.

common_name: Ballet Girl Fuchsia (Double White-and-Cerise Bedding Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in partial shade in cool, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or container mix; Ballet Girl is a Victorian-era (1894) upright bedding and standard fuchsia still widely grown for its crisp bicolor blooms.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil or container mix in partial shade, sheltered from hot afternoon sun. Ballet Girl bears profuse double flowers with a crisp white corolla veined in cerise-pink set against cerise-red sepals, on a vigorous, self-branching, upright-bushy plant that also trains well as a standard. Raised in England in 1894, it has remained a popular exhibition and bedding cultivar for more than a century thanks to its floriferousness and clean bicolor contrast. Pinch young plants to encourage branching, and feed regularly through the growing season to sustain continuous bloom from late spring into fall.

common_name: Leonora Fuchsia (Single Soft Pink Bedding Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in partial shade in cool, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or container mix; Leonora is a mid-20th-century (1961) upright bedding and standard fuchsia awarded the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil or container mix in partial shade, sheltered from hot afternoon sun. Leonora bears an abundance of single, soft rose-pink flowers of uniform color throughout corolla and sepals, giving a neat, candy-pink effect on a vigorous, naturally well-branched, upright-bushy plant that trains readily as a standard. Introduced in 1961, it earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit and remains a widely grown bedding and container fuchsia. Pinch young plants to encourage branching, and feed regularly through the growing season to sustain continuous bloom from late spring into fall.
